Brick

A brick is a type of construction material used to build walls, pavements and other parts of masonry.[1] Strictly, a brick is a unit of shaped clay that has been dried in the sun or fired in a kiln, but the word is also used for blocks of concrete, of lime and sand, and of other materials. Bricks are laid in rows called courses and bound together with mortar.

People have shaped bricks for at least nine thousand years. Sun-dried mud bricks were used in the first towns of the Near East, and fired bricks appear in the Indus Valley by about 3000 BC.[2] Today well over a trillion bricks are produced each year, most of them in China and India.

History

[edit]

Ancient world

[edit]

The oldest known bricks, from Tell Aswad in Syria, were moulded by hand from mud and left to dry in the sun.[3] Builders in Mesopotamia later pressed mud into wooden frames so that every brick had the same size, which made walls easier to lay. Fired bricks were costly because of the fuel they needed, so they were kept for facing walls, drains and floors that had to stand up to water.

Roman bricks

[edit]

The Romans made fired bricks in large numbers and spread the craft across their empire.[4] Roman bricks were usually flatter and wider than modern ones, and many carry the stamp of the legion or the works that made them. Roman builders bound their bricks with lime mortar mixed with volcanic ash, which set hard even under water.

Industrial era

[edit]

In the nineteenth century brick making moved from hand moulding to machines. The Hoffmann kiln, patented in 1858, let bricks be fired continuously, and steam-driven presses could shape thousands of bricks an hour.[5] Cheap bricks made by these works built the terraced housing of many industrial towns.

Manufacture

[edit]

Brick making has four stages: getting the raw material, shaping it, drying it and, for fired bricks, burning it in a kiln.

Mud brick

[edit]

Mud bricks are made of a mixture of earth, water and a binder such as straw or dung, pressed into a mould and dried in the sun for several weeks.[6] They need no fuel, but a wall of mud bricks must be kept dry by a good roof and a raised footing. Adobe is the Spanish name for sun-dried bricks of this kind.

Fired brick

[edit]

Most bricks are made from clay or shale that is crushed, mixed with water to a stiff paste, shaped and then fired. Firing at about 900 to 1,150 °C turns the clay minerals into a hard glassy body that does not soften again in water.[7] The colour of a fired brick depends on the iron in the clay and the air in the kiln: much iron and plenty of air give red bricks, little iron gives cream or yellow ones.

Extruded and pressed bricks

[edit]

In the extrusion method a stiff clay is forced through a die as a long column, which a frame of wires then cuts into bricks.[8] Dry-press bricks are made by pressing a nearly dry clay into steel moulds under high pressure; they have sharp edges and a smooth face.

Types

[edit]

Firebrick

[edit]

Firebricks are made with clays rich in alumina and silica, and they withstand the heat of furnaces, kilns and fireplaces without cracking.[9] They are fired at higher temperatures than ordinary bricks and are laid with a thin refractory mortar.

Calcium-silicate brick

[edit]

Calcium-silicate bricks, also called sand-lime bricks, are made from sand and lime that are pressed and then hardened with steam in an autoclave rather than fired.[10] They are pale grey or white and very even in size.

Concrete brick

[edit]

Concrete bricks and blocks are cast from cement, sand and gravel and cured in moist air.[11] They are cheaper to make than fired bricks in many places, but they shrink slightly as they dry.

Properties

[edit]

A good fired brick has a compressive strength of 10 to 100 megapascals and absorbs less than a fifth of its weight in water.[12] Bricks that absorb too much water can crack when the water in them freezes.

The standard brick in the United Kingdom measures 215 by 102.5 by 65 millimetres, so that two bricks laid side by side with a 10 mm joint are as long as one brick laid end on. In the United States a modular brick measures 194 by 92 by 57 millimetres.[13]

Mortar

[edit]

Bricks are bound together by mortar, a mixture of sand, a binder such as lime or cement, and water.[14] Lime mortar is softer than the bricks it holds, so a wall can move a little without cracking the bricks; old brick walls should be repointed with lime mortar rather than hard cement mortar.

Uses

[edit]

Bricks are used for walls, chimneys, arches, pavements and the linings of furnaces.[15] Because a brick wall stores heat, brick houses stay cool in the day and warm at night in hot dry climates.

Bronze

Bronze
TypeAlloy
Main metalsCopper, tin
Densityabout 8.8 g/cm3
Melting pointabout 950 °C

Bronze is an alloy that is mostly copper, usually with about 12 percent tin and often with other metals such as aluminium, manganese, nickel or zinc, or with arsenic or phosphorus.[16] It is harder than pure copper and melts at a lower temperature, which made it easier to cast into tools, weapons and statues. Bronze gave its name to the Bronze Age, the period when it was the hardest metal in common use.

Etymology

[edit]

The English word comes through French from the Italian bronzo, whose origin is uncertain; one guess ties it to the town of Brindisi, another to a Persian word for copper.[17]

History

[edit]

Discovery

[edit]

The first bronzes were made by smelting copper ores that happened to hold arsenic, which gives a harder metal than copper alone.[18] Tin bronze, which is easier to work and less poisonous to make, replaced arsenical bronze in the Near East by about 2500 BC.

Bronze Age

[edit]

The Bronze Age began in the Near East around 3300 BC and lasted until iron working spread after about 1200 BC.[19] Tin was rare, and the trade in it linked mines in Cornwall, Iberia and Central Asia with the cities of Mesopotamia and Egypt.

Later use

[edit]

Bronze stayed in use for bells, cannon, ship fittings and statues long after iron replaced it for tools.[20] Bronze cannon were preferred at sea for centuries because they did not rust and were less likely to burst than early cast-iron guns.

Composition

[edit]

Modern bronzes are named for the metal added to the copper.

Tin bronze

[edit]

Ordinary tin bronze has 88 percent copper and 12 percent tin.[21] More tin makes the metal harder but more brittle.

Arsenical bronze

[edit]

Arsenical bronze is an alloy of copper with up to 5 percent arsenic, the kind used before tin bronze.[22] Smelting it releases poisonous fumes.

Aluminium bronze

[edit]

Aluminium bronze has between 5 and 11 percent aluminium and resists corrosion in sea water, so it is used for ship propellers and pump parts.[23]

Phosphor bronze

[edit]

Phosphor bronze contains up to 11 percent tin and a fraction of a percent of phosphorus, which makes it springy and tough; it is used for springs, electrical contacts and the wound strings of guitars.[24]

Bell metal

[edit]

Bell metal is a hard bronze with about 22 percent tin.[25] It rings clearly when struck, but it shatters if a bell is dropped or struck too hard when cold.

Properties

[edit]

Bronze is denser than iron and conducts heat well.[26] On exposure to air it forms a thin brown or green layer, called patina, which protects the metal below. Bronze rubbing on steel causes little friction, which is why it is used for bearings and bushes.

Uses

[edit]

Sculpture

[edit]

Bronze is the usual metal for cast statues because it expands slightly as it sets and so fills the fine details of a mould.[27] Most cast statues are made with the lost-wax method, in which a wax model is covered with clay and the wax melted out.

Musical instruments

[edit]

Most good cymbals are made of bell bronze, about 80 percent copper and 20 percent tin, hammered and lathed to shape.[28] Cheaper cymbals are cut from sheets of brass.

Coins and medals

[edit]

Coins called bronze are often made of other copper alloys; the British penny of 1860 was 95 percent copper, 4 percent tin and 1 percent zinc.[29] Third-place medals at the Olympic Games are bronze.

Comparison with brass

[edit]

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, while bronze is copper with tin or another metal.[30] The two are often confused, and some alloys called bronze, such as many architectural bronzes, are really brasses.

Solder

Solder

Melting range (SAC305)217–220 °C

Solder is a fusible metal alloy used to make a lasting bond between metal parts.[31] It is melted so that it wets the surfaces of the joint, and it holds the parts together once it cools. Its melting point is lower than that of the metals it joins, so the parts themselves do not melt.

For most of the twentieth century solder for electronics was an alloy of tin and lead, most often 60/40 or 63/37 by weight. Because lead is toxic, rules in many countries now require lead-free solder in most new electrical goods and in pipes that carry drinking water.[32]

Lead solder

[edit]

Tin–lead solders melt at low temperatures and wet copper easily, which makes them forgiving to use by hand.[33] The 63/37 alloy is eutectic: it melts and freezes at a single temperature, 183 °C, instead of passing through a pasty range, so a joint is less likely to be disturbed while it sets.

A 60/40 solder melts over a range from 183 to about 190 °C. Plumbers once preferred a 50/50 mix, whose wider pasty range let them wipe a joint into shape.

Lead-free solder

[edit]

Lead-free solders are commonly made of tin with about 3 percent silver and 0.5 percent copper; the alloy called SAC305 is 96.5 percent tin.[34] They melt at around 217 to 220 °C, so they need a hotter iron, and the joints they make look duller than those of tin–lead solder.

Solders of pure tin can grow fine metal whiskers over the years, which can short circuits in electronics; small additions of other metals reduce this.

Flux

[edit]

Flux removes the oxide from the metal surfaces and keeps air away while the joint is made.[35] Rosin flux is made from the resin of pine trees and is the usual flux for electronics; much wire solder has a core of it.

Acid fluxes, made with zinc chloride or hydrochloric acid, clean heavily oxidised metal and are used for plumbing and sheet metal, but they corrode electronics and must never be used on circuit boards.

Hard solder

[edit]

Hard solders melt above about 450 °C and are used in brazing.[36] Silver solder, used by jewellers and for joining steel and copper pipes, is an alloy of silver, copper and zinc.

Safety

[edit]

The smoke that rises from soldering comes mainly from the flux, not from the metal, and it can irritate the airways and cause asthma; work with a fume extractor or good ventilation.[37] Lead solder should not be handled near food, and hands should be washed after use, because lead can be swallowed from the skin.

Uses

[edit]

Solder joins the parts of electronic circuits, copper water pipes, sheet-metal work such as gutters, and stained-glass windows.[38] In plumbing, solder for drinking water lines must be lead-free in many countries, and in the United States has been since 1986.

Soap

Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, used for washing, bathing and cleaning.[39] Household soap is made by treating fats or oils with a strong alkali, a reaction called saponification. Soap lets water lift away oil and dirt that water alone cannot remove.

Soap has been made for at least four thousand years; clay tablets from Babylon describe boiling fats with ashes.[40]

How soap works

[edit]

A soap molecule has a long tail that mixes with oil and a charged head that mixes with water.[41] In water the molecules gather around drops of grease in tiny balls called micelles, with their tails inward, and the water carries the micelles away.

Making soap

[edit]

Cold process

[edit]

In the cold process, oils are mixed with a solution of lye and poured into moulds, where the reaction finishes over a day or two; the bars are then left to cure for four to six weeks.[42] Lye is strongly caustic: it burns skin and eyes, so it is handled with gloves and goggles and always added to water, never water to lye.

Hot process

[edit]

In the hot process the mixture is cooked until saponification is complete, so the soap can be used sooner.[43]

Lye

[edit]

Sodium hydroxide gives hard bars and potassium hydroxide gives soft or liquid soap.[44] Lye was once made at home by soaking wood ashes in water and drawing off the brown liquid, which holds potassium carbonate and some potassium hydroxide.

Kinds of soap

[edit]

Castile soap

[edit]

Castile soap is made from olive oil and is named after the region of Castile in Spain.[45] It is mild and lathers less than soaps made with coconut oil.

Liquid soap

[edit]

Liquid soaps are made with potassium hydroxide instead of sodium hydroxide, which gives a soap that dissolves easily.[46] Many products sold as liquid soap are really synthetic detergents.

Laundry soap

[edit]

Laundry soap is often a blend of soap with washing soda and borax, which soften hard water.[47] In hard water soap forms a grey scum with calcium, which is why detergents replaced it for most washing.

Hygiene

[edit]

Washing hands with soap and water for at least twenty seconds removes most germs, and it is one of the best ways to prevent diarrhoea and respiratory infections.[48] Ordinary soap works as well as antibacterial soap for this.

Glass

Glass is a hard, brittle solid without a crystal structure, usually transparent, made by cooling a melt quickly enough that its atoms cannot line up.[49] The most common kind, soda–lime glass, is used for windows, bottles and jars. It is made of about 70 percent silica, from sand, with soda and lime added to lower the melting temperature and make the glass durable.

People have made glass for at least 4,500 years, first as beads and later as vessels, and glass blowing was invented in the eastern Mediterranean in the first century BC.[50]

Manufacture

[edit]

Raw materials

[edit]

The batch for soda–lime glass is sand, soda ash and limestone, often with broken glass called cullet, which melts more easily and saves energy.[51] The batch is melted in a furnace at around 1,500 °C.

Float glass

[edit]

Flat glass for windows is made by the float process, invented by Alastair Pilkington in the 1950s: the molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin, where it spreads into a sheet with flat, smooth faces.[52]

Annealing

[edit]

Glass is cooled slowly in an oven called a lehr to remove the stresses that would make it crack.[53] Toughened glass is instead cooled quickly with jets of air, which leaves its surface in compression; it breaks into small blunt pieces.

Kinds of glass

[edit]

Borosilicate glass

[edit]

Borosilicate glass is made with boron trioxide in place of much of the soda and lime.[54] It expands little when heated, so it survives sudden changes of temperature, and it is used for laboratory glassware and oven dishes.

Lead glass

[edit]

Lead glass, sold as crystal, contains 18 to 40 percent lead oxide, which makes it sparkle and easy to cut.[55] Acidic drinks kept in lead crystal for a long time can take up lead.

Stained glass

[edit]

Coloured glass is made by adding metal oxides to the melt: cobalt gives blue, copper gives green or red, and gold gives a ruby red.[56] Stained-glass windows are pieced together from such glass with strips of lead.

Glass fibre

[edit]

Fibreglass is made of fine fibres of glass, either matted together for insulation or woven and set in resin to make boat hulls and car bodies.[57]

Properties

[edit]

Glass is strong when squeezed but weak when bent or pulled, because cracks start from tiny flaws on its surface.[58] It does not flow at room temperature; old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because the glass has run.

Recycling

[edit]

Glass can be melted and reused without loss of quality any number of times.[59] Bottles are sorted by colour because the colours cannot be separated once melted.

Milk

Milk is a white liquid food produced by the mammary glands of mammals.[60] It is the first food of young mammals, including breastfed human infants, before they can digest solid food. Early milk, called colostrum, carries the mother's antibodies to the young and lowers the risk of many diseases.

Cow's milk is about 87 percent water, with about 4.8 percent lactose, 3.5 percent fat, 3.3 percent protein and 0.7 percent minerals.[61] Its main proteins are casein and whey, and its fat is carried in tiny globules. More than 6 billion people drink milk and eat milk products, and India produces more milk than any other country.

Types

[edit]

Cow's milk

[edit]

Most commercial milk comes from dairy cows, especially the Holstein breed, which can give 30 litres a day.[62] Milk sold in shops is usually a blend of milk from many farms, standardised to a fixed fat content.

Other animals

[edit]

Goat, sheep, buffalo, camel, yak and horse milk are drunk in many regions.[63] Buffalo milk has almost twice the fat of cow's milk and is used for mozzarella and many Indian sweets. Camel milk is lower in fat and is drunk across the Sahara and the Arabian peninsula.

Plant milks

[edit]

Drinks made from soy, oats, almonds, rice or coconut are sold as plant milks.[64] Soy milk is made by soaking and grinding soybeans with water, and oat milk is made from oats blended with water and enzymes. They contain no lactose but also less protein and calcium unless these are added.

Processing

[edit]

Pasteurization

[edit]

Pasteurization heats milk to 72 °C for 15 seconds, or to 63 °C for 30 minutes, to kill harmful bacteria such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli.[65] Raw, unpasteurized milk can carry these germs and is a risk for pregnant women, young children and old people.

Homogenization

[edit]

Homogenization forces milk through small holes under high pressure to break the fat globules into smaller ones, so the cream does not rise.[66] Skimmed milk has had nearly all its fat removed, and semi-skimmed milk is mixed with some cream again to give about 1.7 percent fat.

Powdered and condensed milk

[edit]

Milk powder is made by evaporating milk and then spraying it into hot air until it dries.[67] Sweetened condensed milk is milk with about 60 percent of its water removed and sugar added, which keeps for months without refrigeration.

Milk products

[edit]

Milk is made into butter, cheese, yogurt, cream, ice cream and many other foods.[68] Butter is made by churning cream until the fat separates from the buttermilk.

Cheese is made by curdling milk with rennet or an acid and pressing the curds; most cheese takes about ten litres of milk per kilogram.[69] Yogurt is made by fermenting milk with bacteria that turn lactose into lactic acid.

In tea and coffee, milk is mixed with the hot drink, and in much of South Asia milk is boiled with tea leaves, sugar and spices to make masala chai.

Nutrition

[edit]

Milk is a good source of protein, calcium, vitamin B12 and riboflavin.[70] In many countries milk is fortified with vitamin D, and in some with vitamin A.

Children under one year should not be given cow's milk as their main drink, because it has too little iron and too much protein and salt for them; breast milk or infant formula is recommended.[71]

Lactose intolerance

[edit]

Most adults in the world produce less lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose, after childhood.[72] When they drink milk the lactose ferments in the gut and causes bloating, cramps and diarrhoea. Yogurt and hard cheeses contain less lactose and are often better tolerated.

History

[edit]

People began milking cattle, sheep and goats in South-west Asia about 9,000 years ago.[73] The ability to digest lactose as an adult spread later among herding peoples in Europe, East Africa and the Middle East.

Tooth

A tooth (pl.: teeth) is a hard, calcified structure found in the jaws of many vertebrates and used to break down food.[74] A human tooth is made of four tissues: enamel, dentin, cementum and pulp. The first three are hard and mineralised, while the pulp in the centre holds nerves and blood vessels.

Adults normally have 32 permanent teeth, and children have 20 primary teeth, which begin to come through at about six months of age.[75]

Structure

[edit]

Enamel

[edit]

Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.[76] It is made up of about 96 percent mineral, mostly hydroxyapatite, with water and a little protein making up the rest. Enamel has no living cells, so it cannot repair itself once it is lost to decay or wear.

Dentin

[edit]

Dentin lies under the enamel and is softer and yellower.[77] It consists of about 70 percent mineral, 20 percent organic material and 10 percent water, and is crossed by tiny tubes that carry sensations to the pulp.

Cementum

[edit]

Cementum covers the root of the tooth and anchors it to the jaw through the periodontal ligament.[78]

Pulp

[edit]

The pulp is soft connective tissue with nerves and blood vessels; when decay reaches it, it becomes inflamed and very painful.[79]

Types of teeth

[edit]

Humans have incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, and premolars and molars for grinding.[80] The third molars, or wisdom teeth, often come through between 17 and 25 years of age, and many people do not have room for them.

Development

[edit]

Teeth develop from tooth buds in the jaw long before birth.[81] Primary teeth are shed between the ages of six and twelve as the permanent teeth push up beneath them.

Dental disease

[edit]

Tooth decay

[edit]

Tooth decay is caused by bacteria that turn sugars into acid, which dissolves the enamel.[82] Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, eating less sugar and regular dental check-ups prevent most decay.

Gum disease

[edit]

Plaque left on the teeth hardens into tartar and inflames the gums; in time the bone holding the teeth is lost and they loosen.[83]

Dental restorations

[edit]

Fillings are made of amalgam, a mixture of mercury with silver, tin and copper, or of tooth-coloured composite resin.[84]

Crowns are made of porcelain, metal, or porcelain fused to metal, and cover a damaged tooth completely.

False teeth, or dentures, are made of acrylic resin, sometimes with a metal frame.[85] Dental implants are screws of titanium placed in the jaw bone to hold an artificial tooth.

Teeth of other animals

[edit]

Shark teeth are made of a mineral called fluorapatite and are replaced throughout life, a shark using thousands of teeth in its lifetime.[86]

The tusks of elephants are made of dentin and grow throughout the animal's life.[87] Rodent incisors also grow continuously and are worn down by gnawing.

Snake fangs are hollow or grooved teeth that carry venom.

Mars

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.[88] It is a rocky planet about half the width of Earth, with a thin atmosphere and a surface of red dust that gives it its colour. It has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. They are thought to be captured asteroids, and they are made of dark rock rich in carbon.

Mars has the largest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons, and a canyon system, Valles Marineris, four times as deep as the Grand Canyon.[89] Water ice lies under its polar caps and in its soil.

Internal structure

[edit]

Like Earth, Mars has separated into a dense metallic core, a mantle and a crust.[90] Seismometers on the InSight lander showed that the core is about 1,830 km in radius and is liquid; it is mainly iron and nickel, with about 16 percent sulfur and lighter elements.

The mantle is silicate rock rich in iron, and the crust, about 50 km thick on average, is basalt.[91]

Surface

[edit]

Soil

[edit]

The Martian soil is a fine dust of basalt that is rich in iron oxide, which gives the planet its red colour.[92] It also holds perchlorate salts, which are toxic to people.

Volcanoes

[edit]

Olympus Mons rises about 22 km above the surrounding plains and is a shield volcano like those of Hawaii, built of countless thin lava flows.[93]

Polar caps

[edit]

The polar caps are made of water ice covered in winter by a layer of frozen carbon dioxide, which turns back into gas in spring.[94]

Atmosphere

[edit]

The atmosphere of Mars is about 95 percent carbon dioxide, 2.8 percent nitrogen and 2 percent argon, with traces of oxygen and water vapour.[95] Its pressure at the surface is less than one percent of Earth's.

Dust storms can cover the whole planet for weeks and darken the sky.

Moons

[edit]

Phobos is 22 km across and orbits so close to Mars that it rises in the west and sets in the east twice a day.[96] It is slowly spiralling inward and will break up or crash into Mars in about 50 million years.

Deimos is smaller, about 12 km across, and farther out.[97] Both moons are lumpy and covered in craters and dust.

Exploration

[edit]

Mars has been visited by more spacecraft than any planet except Earth.[98] The first successful landers were the two Viking craft in 1976, and rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance have drilled and analysed its rocks.

Perseverance carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet in 2021.[99]

Gasoline

Gasoline
Density0.71–0.77 kg/L
Energy densityabout 46 MJ/kg
Flash pointabout −43 °C

Gasoline (North American English) or petrol (British and Commonwealth English) is a transparent, flammable liquid used mainly as a fuel in spark-ignition engines.[100] It is a mixture of several hundred hydrocarbons, mostly with four to twelve carbon atoms, made from petroleum by distillation and by reshaping heavier molecules in refineries. Additives are mixed in to improve its burning and to protect engines.

Gasoline is more volatile than diesel fuel and gives off vapour that can ignite far from the liquid; it must be stored only in approved, closed containers away from flames, sparks and living spaces.[101]

Production

[edit]

Petroleum, or crude oil, is a mixture of hydrocarbons found in rock beneath the ground.[102] In a refinery it is heated and separated into fractions by boiling point; the light naphtha fraction becomes the base of gasoline.

Catalytic cracking breaks heavy oil into smaller molecules, and reforming and alkylation turn them into branched molecules that resist knocking.[103] The finished fuel is a blend of streams from several of these units.

One barrel of crude oil, 159 litres, gives about 72 litres of gasoline in a typical American refinery.[104]

Octane rating

[edit]

The octane number measures how well a fuel resists knocking, the early explosion of the fuel and air mixture in a cylinder.[105] Regular gasoline in Europe is rated 95 RON and in the United States 87 by the AKI method; high-compression engines need higher octane.

Additives

[edit]

Tetraethyl lead was added to gasoline from the 1920s to stop knocking, until its harm to health led to bans from the 1970s onward; Algeria was the last country to stop selling leaded petrol, in 2021.[106]

Ethanol is now blended into gasoline in many countries; E10 is 10 percent ethanol by volume.[107] Detergents are added to keep injectors clean.

Safety

[edit]

Gasoline vapour is heavier than air and collects in low places such as pits and basements, where a spark can ignite it.[108] Never use gasoline to start a fire or to clean parts indoors.

Swallowing gasoline or breathing its vapour can cause serious harm; do not siphon it by mouth, and if someone has swallowed it, do not make them vomit and get medical help at once.[109]

Environmental effects

[edit]

Burning one litre of gasoline releases about 2.3 kg of carbon dioxide.[110] Spills poison soil and ground water, and the benzene in gasoline causes cancer.

Concrete

Concrete is a composite material composed of aggregate bonded together with a fluid cement that cures to a solid over time.[111] It is the most widely used building material in the world, and by volume more concrete is made than any other man-made material.

When water is mixed with cement, it forms a paste that coats the sand and gravel and hardens by a chemical reaction called hydration.[112] Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so it is usually reinforced with steel bars.

History

[edit]

The Romans made concrete from lime, volcanic ash and rubble; the dome of the Pantheon, built about AD 125, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.[113] Roman marine concrete, made with ash from the Bay of Naples, grew stronger in sea water.

Portland cement was patented by Joseph Aspdin in 1824, and reinforced concrete was developed in France in the 1850s and 1860s.[114]

Composition

[edit]

Cement

[edit]

Portland cement is made by heating limestone and clay in a kiln to about 1,450 °C and grinding the clinker with a little gypsum.[115] Cement makes up only 10 to 15 percent of a typical concrete mix by mass.

Aggregates

[edit]

Sand and crushed stone or gravel form 60 to 75 percent of the volume of concrete.[116] Clean, hard aggregate of mixed sizes gives the strongest concrete.

Water

[edit]

Too much water makes concrete weaker; a common mix for footings is one part cement, two parts sand and four parts gravel, with about half as much water as cement by weight.[117]

Admixtures

[edit]

Admixtures are chemicals added to the mix to slow or speed setting, to hold tiny air bubbles that resist frost, or to make the mix flow without extra water.[118]

Curing

[edit]

Concrete must be kept moist while it cures; it reaches about 70 percent of its strength in seven days and its design strength in 28 days.[119] Concrete that dries out or freezes in its first days never reaches full strength.

Reinforced concrete

[edit]

Reinforced concrete is concrete with steel bars or mesh cast inside it, which carry the tension that the concrete cannot.[120] The steel must be covered by enough concrete to keep it from rusting.

Mortar and grout

[edit]

Mortar is a mixture of sand, cement or lime, and water, without the coarse aggregate of concrete.[121] It is used to bind bricks and stones.

Environmental impact

[edit]

Making cement releases about 8 percent of the world's carbon dioxide emissions, from the fuel burned in the kilns and from the limestone itself as it breaks down.[122]

Safety

[edit]

Wet concrete is strongly alkaline and can cause chemical burns to skin and eyes; wear gloves, boots and eye protection, and wash it off skin at once.[123]

Ice

Ice
Density (0 °C)0.917 g/cm3
Melting point0 °C at 1 atm
Crystal structureHexagonal (ice Ih)

Ice is water that has frozen into a solid.[124] Depending on the presence of impurities such as particles of soil or bubbles of air, it can appear transparent or a more or less opaque bluish-white colour. Ordinary ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats; about nine tenths of an iceberg lies below the surface.

Water freezes into ice at 0 °C at sea-level pressure, though very pure water can be cooled below this without freezing.[125] Ice covers about a tenth of the land on Earth, in glaciers and ice sheets, and much of the polar oceans in winter.

Physical properties

[edit]

In ordinary ice each water molecule is held by hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in an open hexagonal lattice, which is why ice takes more room than the water it came from.[126] Water expands by about 9 percent as it freezes, enough to split rocks and burst pipes.

At least nineteen other crystal forms of ice are known, made under high pressure in laboratories or found deep inside icy moons.[127]

Natural ice

[edit]

Sea ice

[edit]

Sea ice forms when the surface of the sea freezes; it consists of fresh-water ice crystals with pockets of salty brine between them, and it slowly loses its salt as it ages.[128]

Glaciers

[edit]

Glacier ice is made from snow that is buried and pressed by later snowfall until its air is squeezed out.[129] Old glacier ice is dense and blue because it absorbs red light.

Hail

[edit]

Hailstones form in thunderstorms as drops of water freeze in layers onto small particles carried up and down by the wind.[130]

Uses

[edit]

Cooling

[edit]

Before refrigerators, ice cut from lakes in winter was stored in ice houses packed with sawdust and sold in summer; the price of ice fell as the trade grew.[131] A modern device such as an ice maker freezes water in a mould and drops the cubes into a bin.

Food

[edit]

Ice cream is made of milk, cream and sugar, churned while it freezes so that the ice crystals stay small.[132] Shaved ice mixed with sweet syrup is sold on the streets of many hot countries.

Ice used in drinks should be made from safe drinking water; ice made from untreated water can spread cholera, typhoid and other diseases.[133]

Sport

[edit]

Ice skates are made of a steel blade fixed to a boot.[134] Ice hockey pucks are made of vulcanised rubber and are frozen before games so they bounce less.

Safety on ice

[edit]

Ice on lakes and rivers is safe to walk on only when it is thick enough: at least 10 cm of clear, new ice for one person on foot, and much more for vehicles.[135] Ice over moving water, near inlets and under snow is thinner and weaker.

A person who falls through ice should turn back toward the way they came, put their arms flat on the ice and kick to slide out, then roll away rather than stand up; call for help and get them warm at once.[136]

Dry ice

[edit]

Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide, not frozen water; it turns straight into gas at −78.5 °C.[137] It can burn the skin, and in a closed room or car its gas can suffocate.

Atmosphere of Earth

Atmosphere of Earth

Nitrogen78.08%

Argon0.93%
Carbon dioxideabout 0.04%

The atmosphere of Earth is the layer of gases, known together as air, held around the planet by its gravity.[138] It protects life by absorbing ultraviolet light, warming the surface by trapping heat, and evening out the difference between day and night temperatures.

By volume, dry air contains 78.08 percent nitrogen, 20.95 percent oxygen, 0.93 percent argon, about 0.04 percent carbon dioxide and small traces of other gases.[139] Air near the ground also holds water vapour, on average about 1 percent at sea level.

Layers

[edit]

Troposphere

[edit]

The troposphere, the lowest layer, holds about 80 percent of the mass of the atmosphere and nearly all its water vapour; it is where weather happens.[140] It is about 12 km thick on average, thinner at the poles and thicker at the equator.

Stratosphere

[edit]

Above the troposphere, the stratosphere holds the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet light.[141] Airliners fly near its base, above most of the weather.

Higher layers

[edit]

The mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere thin out gradually into space; there is no sharp upper edge, though the Kármán line at 100 km is often used as one.[142]

Pressure

[edit]

Air pressure at sea level averages 101.3 kilopascals, the weight of the air above pressing down.[143] It halves roughly every 5.5 km of height, which is why climbers on the highest mountains carry bottled oxygen.

Air pollution

[edit]

Air pollution consists of gases and fine particles released by burning fuel, by industry, by farming and by fires.[144] Fine particles called PM2.5 travel deep into the lungs and are linked to heart disease, stroke and lung cancer.

Indoor air in homes that cook over open fires of wood, dung or coal is often far dirtier than city air outside; a chimney or a cleaner stove greatly reduces the smoke.[145]

Dairy farms and fertilised fields release ammonia, which is mixed with other pollutants in the air to form fine particles.[146]

Air in daily life

[edit]

Compressed air is used to drive tools and to inflate tyres; a tyre repair kit is made of a sealant and a small pump.[147]

Hair dryers and fans move air but do not cool it; they cool people by speeding up the evaporation of sweat.

Liquid air is produced by cooling air until it condenses, and it is separated into pure nitrogen, oxygen and argon by distillation.[148]

Evolution

[edit]

Earth's first atmosphere was mostly hydrogen and helium and was lost to space.[149] Oxygen built up only after cyanobacteria began releasing it about 2.4 billion years ago, in the Great Oxidation Event.

Honey

Honey is a sweet and thick food that honey bees and some related insects make from the nectar of flowers.[150] The bees collect nectar, change it with enzymes and evaporate much of its water, and store the result in wax cells as food for the colony through winter. Honey is about 80 percent sugars, mainly fructose and glucose, and about 17 percent water.

It is often mixed with lemon and hot water as a home remedy for a sore throat or cough.[151] Honey must never be given to babies under twelve months old, because it can carry spores of the bacterium that causes infant botulism.

Production

[edit]

A colony of honey bees may make 25 to 50 kilograms of honey a year more than it needs, which the beekeeper takes.[152] The combs are uncapped with a hot knife, spun in an extractor and the honey is strained.

Most honey sold in shops is a blend of honeys from many hives and often from several countries.[153]

Varieties

[edit]

Monofloral honey

[edit]

Monofloral honey is produced from the nectar of mainly one kind of plant, such as clover, orange blossom or heather, and has its own taste and colour.[154] Manuka honey is produced from the nectar of the manuka tree of New Zealand.

Creamed honey

[edit]

Creamed honey is made by mixing a little fine crystallised honey into liquid honey and keeping it cool, so that it sets into a smooth spread.[155]

Honeydew honey

[edit]

Honeydew honey is made from the sweet secretions of aphids and other insects that feed on plant sap, rather than from nectar.[156] It is darker and less sweet.

Properties

[edit]

Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution, and it crystallises in time, especially in the cold; warming the jar gently in water makes it liquid again.[157]

Because it has little water and is acidic, honey keeps almost indefinitely if it is sealed; edible honey has been found in ancient Egyptian tombs.[158]

Uses

[edit]

Honey is used as a sweetener in drinks, baking and sauces.[159] Mead is made by fermenting honey with water and sometimes fruit or spices.

In cooking, honey is mixed with mustard, soy sauce or vinegar to glaze meats, and honey mixed with yogurt is a common breakfast.[160]

Medical-grade honey is used in dressings for some wounds and burns, under the care of a health worker.[161]

Adulteration

[edit]

Honey is often adulterated by being mixed with cheaper syrups of corn, rice or beet sugar; tests of pollen and sugar ratios can detect it.[162]

Tar

Tar is a dark brown or black viscous liquid of hydrocarbons and free carbon, obtained from many kinds of organic material by heating them without air, a process called destructive distillation.[163] It can be produced from coal, wood, petroleum or peat.

Tar should not be confused with bitumen, which is the heavy residue of crude oil, although the two words are often used for each other.[164]

Types

[edit]

Coal tar

[edit]

Coal tar is a by-product of making coke and coal gas.[165] It is a complex mixture of hundreds of compounds, and some of them, such as benzopyrene, cause cancer.

Wood tar

[edit]

Wood tar, or pine tar, is made by heating pine wood slowly in a covered pit or kiln.[166] It was used for thousands of years to waterproof the hulls and ropes of wooden ships.

Uses

[edit]

Tarmac is a mixture of crushed stone and tar, rolled flat to make a road surface; the name is now used for any road surface of asphalt.[167]

Mortar is a mixture of sand and lime; in medieval Scandinavia it was sometimes mixed with tar to make it resist water.[168]

From the start, pine tar was used on skis and boats, and roofers still use tar paper, which is made of felt soaked in tar.[169]

Coal tar soaps and shampoos are used to treat psoriasis and dandruff under medical advice.[170]

Tobacco tar

[edit]

Tar is also the name for the sticky residue of tobacco smoke, which holds most of its cancer-causing chemicals.[171]

Safety

[edit]

Hot tar causes deep burns; cool a tar burn with cold running water for at least 20 minutes and do not try to peel the tar off the skin; get medical care.[172]

Oral rehydration therapy

Oral rehydration therapy
Other namesOral rehydration solution (ORS)
Used forDehydration from diarrhoea

Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially that due to diarrhoea.[173] It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium. Oral rehydration therapy can also be given by a nasogastric tube.

The World Health Organization's oral rehydration salts (ORS) come as a powder in a sachet that is dissolved in one litre of clean water.[174] The low-osmolarity formula holds sodium chloride, glucose, potassium chloride and trisodium citrate; the glucose helps the gut take up the sodium and the water with it. Zinc supplements are given alongside it to children.

Medical uses

[edit]

ORT is the treatment of choice for mild and moderate dehydration in people of all ages.[175] Doctors and health workers judge dehydration by thirst, sunken eyes, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies and skin that goes back slowly when pinched.

Severe dehydration, with sleepiness, inability to drink or very fast breathing, needs urgent care at a health facility, usually with fluids into a vein.[176]

Several factors, such as vomiting, refusal to drink, or a very high stool output, make ORT harder; small sips every one or two minutes usually work even when a child is vomiting.[177]

Preparation

[edit]

Each sachet must be dissolved in the exact volume of water printed on it; too little water makes the solution too salty, which can be harmful.[178]

Where sachets are not available, health authorities have described a home-made solution; a health worker should show how to make it, because mistakes in the amounts are common and dangerous.[179]

Made-up solution should be used within 24 hours and then thrown away.[180]

History

[edit]

Large trials in refugee camps in the 1970s showed that ORT cut deaths from cholera from about 30 percent to under 4 percent.[181] It is thought to have saved tens of millions of lives.

Society and culture

[edit]

The sachets are cheap, and UNICEF supplies hundreds of millions each year.[182] They are often packed in bright colors so that families recognise them.

Sun

Sun

Mass1.989 × 10^30 kg

The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System.[183] It is a massive, nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma, heated to incandescence by nuclear fusion reactions in its core, and it radiates energy mainly as visible light and infrared. It is by far the most important source of energy for life on Earth.

The Sun is about 73 percent hydrogen by mass and about 25 percent helium, with much smaller quantities of heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon and iron.[184] It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a region of a large molecular cloud.

Structure

[edit]

Core

[edit]

The core extends from the centre to about a quarter of the solar radius, and it is there that hydrogen is fused into helium at about 15 million kelvin.[185] Every second the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of matter into energy.

Radiative and convective zones

[edit]

Energy leaves the core as light that is absorbed and re-emitted so many times that it takes tens of thousands of years to cross the radiative zone.[186] In the outer third of the Sun, hot gas rises and cool gas sinks in great convection cells.

Photosphere

[edit]

The photosphere, the visible surface, has a temperature of about 5,800 K.[187] It has a grainy look made of convection cells about 1,000 km across.

Corona

[edit]

The corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere, which is heated to over a million kelvin by processes that are still not fully understood.[188] The corona consists of thin plasma that streams away as the solar wind.

Sunlight

[edit]

Sunlight at the top of Earth's atmosphere carries about 1,361 watts per square metre.[189] At the surface, sunlight consists of about 53 percent infrared, 44 percent visible light and 3 percent ultraviolet.

Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.

Activity

[edit]

Sunspots

[edit]

Sunspots are darker, cooler areas of the photosphere where strong magnetic fields block convection.[190] A sunspot consists of a dark centre, the umbra, surrounded by a lighter penumbra; their number rises and falls in an eleven-year cycle.

Flares

[edit]

Solar flares and coronal mass ejections fling charged particles into space; large ones can disturb radio and satellites and cause auroras.[191]

Observation and safety

[edit]

Never look directly at the Sun, even during a partial eclipse, and never through binoculars or a telescope without a proper solar filter; it can cause permanent eye damage within seconds.[192] Sunglasses are not safe for this.

Eclipse glasses are made of special filter film that meets the ISO 12312-2 standard.[193] A pinhole projector, made with two pieces of card, is a safe way to watch an eclipse.

Sunscreen is made with compounds that absorb or reflect ultraviolet light, such as zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.[194]

Life cycle

[edit]

The Sun is about halfway through its life on the main sequence.[195] In about five billion years it will swell into a red giant, and then shed its outer layers and end as a white dwarf made mostly of carbon and oxygen.

Saliva

Saliva is an extracellular fluid produced and secreted by the salivary glands in the mouth.[196] In humans, saliva is around 99 percent water, plus electrolytes, mucus, white blood cells, epithelial cells, antimicrobial agents and enzymes such as amylase and lipase. The enzymes in saliva begin the digestion of starches and fats.

Saliva also cleans the mouth and teeth, protects them from bacteria, and makes food easier to swallow.[197] A healthy adult produces about 0.75 to 1.5 litres a day.

Function

[edit]

Digestion

[edit]

During chewing, saliva is mixed with food to form a soft mass called a bolus that can be swallowed.[198] Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into sugar, which is why bread tastes sweeter the longer it is chewed.

Protection

[edit]

Saliva neutralises acids made by bacteria in dental plaque, and its calcium and phosphate help repair early damage to the enamel.[199] People who produce little saliva get more tooth decay and mouth infections.

Production

[edit]

Three pairs of major glands, the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands, make most saliva, with hundreds of minor glands in the lining of the mouth.[200] Flow increases at the sight, smell or thought of food and falls almost to nothing during sleep.

Dry mouth

[edit]

Dry mouth, or xerostomia, is caused by many medicines, by radiation treatment of the head and neck, by dehydration and by some diseases such as Sjögren syndrome.[201]

Artificial saliva is made of carboxymethylcellulose or similar thickeners with salts, and it is used to relieve dry mouth.[202] Chewing sugar-free gum and sipping water also help.

Diagnostic use

[edit]

Saliva tests can detect hormones, drugs and some infections; a saliva sample is mixed with a reagent in a small tube.[203]

In other animals

[edit]

The saliva of some animals has special uses: vampire bat saliva holds a substance that stops blood clotting, and swiftlets build nests made of their own hardened saliva, which are eaten as bird's nest soup.[204] The saliva of the Komodo dragon is mixed with venom from glands in the jaw.

Seawater

Seawater, or sea water, is water from a sea or ocean.[205] On average, seawater in the world's oceans has a salinity of about 3.5 percent: every kilogram holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts, mostly sodium and chloride ions, with magnesium, sulfate, calcium and potassium. It is denser than fresh water and freezes at about −2 °C.

Salinity

[edit]

Salinity is highest in warm, enclosed seas where much water evaporates, such as the Red Sea at about 4 percent, and lowest where rivers and melting ice add fresh water, as in the Baltic.[206] Brackish water in estuaries is seawater mixed with river water.

Drinking seawater

[edit]

People must not drink seawater: the kidneys cannot make urine saltier than about 2 percent, so drinking it makes a person lose more water than they took in, and it leads to dehydration and death.[207] Castaways have died from it.

Desalination

[edit]

Desalination removes the salt from seawater by distillation or reverse osmosis.[208] Brine from desalination plants is a solution of salts about twice as strong as seawater and must be released with care.

A simple solar still, made of a dark basin under a sloping sheet of glass or plastic, evaporates seawater and collects the fresh condensate; it yields only a few litres a day per square metre.[209]

Uses

[edit]

Sea salt is produced by evaporating seawater in shallow ponds.[210] Seawater is mixed with fresh water to cool power stations, and some cities flush toilets with it.

Artificial seawater for aquariums is a mixture of salts sold as a powder and dissolved in purified water.[211]

Bone

A bone is a rigid organ that makes up part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.[212] Bones protect the organs, make red and white blood cells, store minerals and support the body. Bone tissue is about 60 percent mineral, mainly calcium phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite, 30 percent collagen protein and 10 percent water. The adult human skeleton has 206 bones.

Structure

[edit]

Compact bone

[edit]

Compact bone forms the hard outer shell of bones and gives them strength.[213]

Spongy bone

[edit]

Spongy bone, found at the ends of long bones and inside vertebrae, is a lattice of thin struts filled with bone marrow.[214]

Bone marrow

[edit]

Bone marrow is a soft tissue in the hollow of bones; red marrow makes blood cells, and yellow marrow consists of fat cells.[215]

Fractures

[edit]

A broken bone, or fracture, needs to be kept still with a splint until it can be seen by a health worker; do not try to straighten a badly bent limb.[216] A fracture where the bone breaks the skin is an emergency because of the risk of infection.

Plaster casts are made of gauze soaked in plaster of Paris, and fibreglass casts are made of glass fibres in resin.[217]

Bone health

[edit]

Bones need calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise to stay strong.[218] In osteoporosis, bones lose density and break easily, mostly in older women.

Uses of bone

[edit]

Bone meal, a fertiliser, is made from crushed animal bones.[219] Bone china is a porcelain made with bone ash mixed with clay.

Bone glue is produced by boiling bones and hides.

Mumbai

Mumbai

Mumbai, known until 1995 as Bombay, is the capital of the Indian state of Maharashtra and the country's largest city, with more than twenty million people in its wider region. It is India's centre of finance and film, a city of colonial stone buildings, slums, towers and a long sea front.

Understand

The city grew on seven islands that were joined by land reclamation from the eighteenth century onward. The Portuguese held the islands first and passed them to the English crown in 1661 as part of a royal dowry; the East India Company then built its western port here.

Today the island city is the old core in the south, around the Fort district and Colaba, while the suburbs stretch north for more than forty kilometres. Most visitors stay in the south, where the museums, the Gateway of India and the best colonial buildings are.

The monsoon arrives in early June and brings very heavy rain until September; streets and railway lines flood several times each season. The best time to visit is from November to February, when days are warm and dry.

The tourist office of the state government is opposite Churchgate station and gives out free city maps.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Orientation

Locals give directions by railway station rather than by street address, and nearly every neighbourhood is named after its station. The Western line runs up the west side of the city from Churchgate, and the Central line runs from Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus up the east side.

Get in

By plane

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM) is 25 km north of the old city and is one of the busiest in Asia. Terminal 2 handles all international and most domestic flights.

Prepaid taxi counters inside the arrival hall charge a fixed fare to each part of the city, about ₹700 to Colaba; the ride takes one to two hours depending on traffic. App cabs pick up from a marked bay outside the terminal.

The Metro Line 3 station under Terminal 2 links the airport with the south of the city in about 50 minutes.

By train

Long-distance trains arrive at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) and Mumbai Central in the south, and at Lokmanya Tilak Terminus and Bandra Terminus in the suburbs. The overnight Rajdhani Express from New Delhi takes about sixteen hours.

Book long-distance tickets weeks ahead; foreign tourists can buy from a small quota of seats at the tourist counter at CSMT on the day.

By bus

State and private buses connect the city with Pune, Goa and Gujarat. Most private sleeper buses leave from the roads around Dadar and Sion in the evening.

Get around

Traffic is slow at most hours, and the suburban trains are the fastest way to cover long distances.

By suburban train

The suburban railway carries more than seven million passengers a day on three lines. Trains run from about 4AM to 1AM; avoid the rush hours if you can, when doors are crowded and people hang from the carriages.

Every train has carriages reserved for women, marked on the platform. A ticket costs a few rupees; buy it at the window or with the official app before you board, as fines are heavy.

By taxi

Black-and-yellow taxis run on meters in the island city; check that the driver starts the meter. App cabs cost about the same and need no bargaining.

By auto-rickshaw

Auto-rickshaws are not allowed in the island city south of Bandra and Sion, but they are the usual way to get about the suburbs. They run on meters.

By ferry

Ferries leave from the Gateway of India for Elephanta Island every half hour in the morning; the crossing takes about an hour.

See

The Gateway of India, a basalt arch on the waterfront at Apollo Bunder, was built to mark a royal visit in 1911 and finished in 1924.

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus is a Gothic railway station of 1888 and a World Heritage Site; its towers and carvings are best seen from the road junction opposite.

The Elephanta Caves, on an island an hour away by ferry, hold rock-cut temples to Shiva from the fifth to the eighth century.

  • Town Museum, Market Street. A small museum of local history in a merchant's house, with old maps, costumes and photographs of the town a century ago; labels are in English and the local language.
  • Market Hall, the main square. A covered market hall of iron and glass from the 1890s, busiest early in the morning when the fishmongers and fruit sellers set up.

Do

Walk the seafront promenade of Marine Drive at sunset, when the curve of street lights is called the Queen's Necklace.

Watch a Hindi film in one of the old single-screen cinemas, where the audience cheers and sings along.

  • Market cooking class, the main square. Take a cooking class in a family kitchen, with a trip to the market to buy the ingredients first.
  • Riverside cycling, the north gate. Hire a bicycle and ride the flat riverside path out to the villages and back in a morning.
  • City stadium, the cathedral square. Watch a football match at the city stadium, where tickets are cheap and the crowd is loud.

Buy

Cash is still common in small shops, but cards are taken in malls and most restaurants, and many stalls take payment by phone. ATMs are everywhere in the south.

Colaba Causeway is lined with stalls selling clothes, jewellery and souvenirs; bargain hard.

Eat

Street food is the heart of the city's cooking: vada pav, a spiced potato fritter in a bun, is the classic snack, and pav bhaji, a buttery vegetable mash with bread, is a close second.

Eat where locals queue and the food is cooked in front of you.

Budget

  • Morning Bakery, Station Road, mains US$11. Bakery and coffee shop with pastries, sandwiches and free wifi, handy for breakfast before an early bus.

Drink

Bars and cafes stay open late in the centre, and the local beer is cheap.

  • The Lantern Pub, the main square. A small pub with live music on Friday and Saturday nights and cheap local beer on tap.

Sleep

Rooms are expensive by Indian standards. Colaba has the most budget guesthouses, while the business hotels are near the airport and in Bandra-Kurla.

Budget

  • Teacher's House, the north gate, from US$55. A quiet guesthouse in a side street run by a retired teacher; book ahead in the high season.
  • Station Business Hotel, the cathedral square, from US$70. Business hotel near the main station with small but clean rooms and a buffet breakfast.

Stay safe

Mumbai is fairly safe for its size, but pickpockets work the crowded trains and markets. Keep your phone out of sight near the train doors.

During heavy monsoon rain stay off the roads and the railway when flooding is announced.

Stay healthy

Drink bottled or filtered water. Dengue and malaria are spread by mosquitoes during and after the monsoon; use repellent.

Connect

Prepaid SIM cards are sold at the airport and at phone shops in the centre; bring your passport, which is needed to register the card.

Most hotels, cafes and many restaurants have free wifi.

Go next

Pune — a university city on the plateau, three hours by train or road.

Goa — beaches to the south, an overnight train or a short flight.

Lonavala — a hill station on the way to Pune, busy with day trippers in the monsoon.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2024-01/A/Ho_Chi_:
Ho Chi Minh City

Ho Chi Minh City

Ho Chi Minh City, still called Saigon by most of its people, is the largest city of Vietnam and its busiest port, a fast, loud, motorbike-filled place on the Saigon River in the south of the country.

Understand

The city was the capital of South Vietnam until 1975 and was renamed after the war; the old name lives on in the name of the central district, the river, the beer and the main railway station.

The climate is tropical: hot all year, with a wet season from May to November when short, heavy storms come most afternoons. The dry season from December to April is the most comfortable time for a trip.

District 1 holds the colonial centre, the main hotels and the backpacker area around Pham Ngu Lao street; District 3 is quieter, and District 5 is the old Chinese quarter of Cho Lon.

Tourist information is limited; the free maps at the big hotels are the best on offer.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Tan Son Nhat International Airport (SGN) is 7 km north of District 1. Bus 109 runs from the arrivals hall to the Ben Thanh market and the backpacker area for 20,000 dong; the trip takes 45 minutes.

Metered taxis from the official rank take about 30 minutes to District 1 and cost around 200,000 dong; ignore the drivers who approach you inside the hall.

A new terminal at Long Thanh, 40 km east, is planned to take most international flights.

By train

Saigon railway station, in District 3, is the end of the line from Hanoi; the fastest trains take about 33 hours for the full journey, and sleeper berths sell out at holidays.

By bus

Long-distance buses use the Mien Dong terminal for the north and the Mien Tay terminal for the Mekong Delta. Sleeper buses to Da Lat take about seven hours.

Buses from Phnom Penh in Cambodia take about six hours and cross the border at Moc Bai; Cambodian visas are sold at the border.

Get around

Motorbikes fill every street, and crossing the road is the first skill to learn: walk slowly and steadily, and the riders will flow around you.

By motorbike taxi

Motorbike taxis, called xe om, wait on most corners; agree the fare first, or book one through an app, which shows the price before you ride.

By bus

City buses are cheap and air-conditioned but slow, and the routes are hard to learn without the official app.

By metro

Metro Line 1 runs east from Ben Thanh to Thu Duc and the city's edge.

By boat

A river bus runs from Bach Dang pier along the Saigon River to Thu Duc, with views of the city's skyline.

See

The War Remnants Museum tells the story of the war from the Vietnamese side; its photographs are hard to forget.

The Reunification Palace, the former presidential palace, is kept as it was in 1975, with its tanks in the garden.

The Cu Chi Tunnels, 60 km north-west, are a network of underground passages used in the war; tours leave from District 1 every morning, and public bus 13 goes there from Ben Thanh for a fraction of the price.

Arusha

Arusha

Arusha is a city in northern Tanzania at the foot of Mount Meru, and the starting point for safaris to the Serengeti, the Ngorongoro Crater and Tarangire.

Understand

The town grew as a German garrison and later a coffee-growing centre. Its cool climate, at 1,400 m, makes it pleasant all year, though it rains heavily in April and May.

Nearly every visitor passes through on the way to the parks, and the streets are full of safari companies and touts. Book a safari with a licensed operator; ask to see the licence from the Tanzania Association of Tour Operators.

The Tanzania Tourist Board has an information office on Boma Road, next to the clock tower, with lists of licensed operators and free maps.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Kilimanjaro International Airport (JRO) lies 50 km east, between Arusha and Moshi. Shuttle buses meet the main flights and take about an hour to the town centre; a taxi costs about US$50.

The small Arusha Airport, 8 km west, handles light aircraft to the parks and to Zanzibar.

By bus

Shuttle buses run twice a day to Nairobi in about six hours, crossing the border at Namanga.

Big buses from Dar es Salaam take nine to ten hours and arrive at the central bus stand.

Get around

The centre is small enough to walk by day.

By dala-dala

Minibuses called dala-dalas run along the main roads for a few hundred shillings; they are crowded and stop anywhere.

By taxi

Taxis wait near the clock tower and the bus stand; agree on the fare before you set off.

Motorbike taxis, called boda-bodas, are quick but often crash; insist on a helmet.

See

Arusha National Park, 25 km east, has giraffes, colobus monkeys and the slopes of Mount Meru, and it can be seen in a day without a long drive. Take a dala-dala to Usa River and a taxi from there to the Momella gate, or join a day tour.

The Cultural Heritage Centre on the road west of town sells carvings and has a gallery of Tanzanian art.

pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2024-01/A/Delhi:
Delhi

Delhi

Delhi is India's capital territory, a sprawling metropolis of more than thirty million people that holds both the walled Mughal city of Old Delhi and the broad avenues of New Delhi, built by the British in the 1920s.

Understand

Cities have stood on this stretch of the Yamuna river for three thousand years, and the ruins of at least seven of them are scattered across the modern territory. Shah Jahan built the walled city of Shahjahanabad, now called Old Delhi, in the seventeenth century, with the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid at its heart.

New Delhi, the seat of the national government, was laid out south of the old city by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. Its centre is Connaught Place, a ring of white colonnaded buildings with shops and offices.

Summers are fiercely hot, with days above 45 °C in May and June, and winters bring cold, smoggy mornings. October to March is the usual season for a trip, but air pollution is at its worst in November.

The India Tourism office at 88 Janpath gives free maps and lists of approved guides; be wary of the many private offices that call themselves tourist offices.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Districts

Paharganj, opposite New Delhi railway station, is the backpacker district, with cheap rooms and constant noise. South Delhi holds most of the better hotels, the embassies and Hauz Khas village.

Get in

By plane

Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) is 16 km south-west of Connaught Place. The Airport Express metro line runs from Terminal 3 to New Delhi railway station in about 20 minutes, every ten minutes from 4:45AM to 11:30PM.

Prepaid taxi booths in the arrival halls sell fixed-fare rides; a ride to Connaught Place costs around ₹500 and takes 40 minutes or more.

By train

New Delhi railway station, next to Paharganj, is the main station for trains from Mumbai, Kolkata and Agra. Old Delhi station, in the walled city, serves many trains to Rajasthan and Punjab; Hazrat Nizamuddin serves the south.

Ignore anyone at the station entrance who says your train is cancelled or that the ticket office has moved; it is a scam to lead you to a private agency. The foreign tourist booking office is on the first floor of New Delhi station.

By bus

Interstate buses use the Kashmere Gate terminal near Old Delhi; buses to Agra, Jaipur and the hill stations leave every few minutes.

Get around

Delhi is spread out, and most trips need some form of transport.

By metro

The metro is clean, cheap and the quickest way across the city, with more than 250 stations. The first carriage of every train is for women only. Buy a smart card or a token at the station; bags are scanned at every entrance.

By auto-rickshaw

Green-and-yellow auto-rickshaws are everywhere; drivers rarely use the meter, so agree the fare before you set off or book through an app.

By cycle-rickshaw

In the lanes of the old city, cycle-rickshaws are the only practical transport after walking.

By taxi

App cabs are reliable and the drivers rarely argue about the fare. Black-and-yellow taxis are now rare.

The Red Fort, the Mughal palace of red sandstone, is open daily except Monday.

Humayun's Tomb, a garden tomb of 1570, was a model for the Taj Mahal.

Qutub Minar, a 73 m tower of the twelfth century, stands in the far south of the city; take the metro to Qutub Minar station and an auto-rickshaw for the last kilometre.

Saint Petersburg

Saint Petersburg

Saint Petersburg, often shortened to St. Petersburg and called Leningrad from 1924 to 1991, is Russia's second city, built on the islands of the Neva delta at the head of the Gulf of Finland.

Understand

Peter the Great founded the city in 1703 as a port and a window on Europe, and it was the capital of the Russian Empire for two centuries. Its centre of canals, palaces and pastel facades is a World Heritage Site.

In June the sun barely sets, and the White Nights festival fills the embankments with people at midnight. Winters are long and dark, with the canals frozen from December to March.

The bridges over the Neva are raised for shipping every night from April to November, roughly between 1AM and 5AM, so plan how you will get home if you are on the wrong island.

The city tourist information centre on Sadovaya Street has English-speaking staff and free maps.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Pulkovo Airport (LED) is 20 km south of the centre. Bus 39 runs to Moskovskaya metro station every 15 minutes, and the trip on to the centre takes about an hour in all.

Official taxis can be ordered at the desk in the arrivals hall for a fixed price.

By train

Naples

Naples

Naples (Italian: Napoli) is the capital of Campania and the largest city of southern Italy, a crowded, noisy and hugely rewarding port on a bay overlooked by Mount Vesuvius.

Understand

Greek settlers founded the city as Neapolis, the new city, in the sixth century BC, and its historic centre still follows the grid of Greek streets. Naples was the capital of a kingdom until 1861.

The city has a reputation for petty crime that is out of date in most districts, though bag snatching still happens. The historic centre, the Spanish Quarter and the seafront are all busy late into the night.

The tourist information point in Piazza del Gesù sells the Campania ArteCard, which covers transport and museum entry.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

By train

Napoli Centrale, in Piazza Garibaldi, is the main station. High-speed trains from Rome take about 70 minutes, and from Milan about four and a half hours.

By boat

By metro

Line 1 of the metro links the central station with the historic centre and the hills of Vomero; its stations are decorated by modern artists, and Toledo station is worth a visit for itself.

By funicular

Four funicular railways climb from the lower city to Vomero and Posillipo.

Kuala Lumpur

Kuala Lumpur

Kuala Lumpur, known to everyone as KL, is the capital of Malaysia, a city of skyscrapers, markets and Malay, Chinese and Indian neighbourhoods, best known for the twin Petronas Towers.

Understand

KL began in 1857 as a tin-mining camp where the Klang and Gombak rivers meet, and the name means muddy confluence. It grew fast under British rule and became the capital of the independent federation in 1957.

The weather is hot and humid all year, with heavy afternoon thunderstorms, most of all from October to March.

Cusco

Cusco

Cusco (also spelled Cuzco, and Qosqo in Quechua) is a city high in the Andes of southern Peru, once the capital of the Inca Empire and now the gateway to Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley.

Understand

The Incas built their capital in the shape of a puma, with the fortress of Sacsayhuamán as its head. The Spanish took the city in 1533 and built churches and mansions on the fitted stone walls of Inca palaces and temples, many of which can still be seen in the streets around the Plaza de Armas.

The city stands at 3,400 m. Most visitors feel short of breath, and many get headaches, poor sleep or nausea for the first day or two; this is altitude sickness. Take the first day slowly, drink plenty of water, and avoid alcohol until you feel well.

The dry season, from May to September, has clear skies and cold nights, and it is the busiest time. From December to March it rains most afternoons, and the Inca Trail is closed in February for maintenance.

iPerú, the national tourist information service, has an office on the Plaza de Armas and a desk in the airport arrivals hall.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport (CUZ) is 5 km south-east of the centre and has frequent flights from Lima, which take about 80 minutes. A taxi to the Plaza de Armas takes 20 minutes; use the official taxi desk inside the terminal.

By bus

Buses from Lima take about 22 hours, from Arequipa about ten, and from Puno on Lake Titicaca about seven; they arrive at the Terminal Terrestre, 2 km south of the centre.

By train

A tourist train runs between Puno and Cusco across the high plateau three or four times a week; the journey takes about ten hours and includes meals.

Get around

The historic centre is compact and best seen on foot, though its steep cobbled streets are hard work at this altitude.

By taxi

Taxis are cheap and plentiful; a ride within the centre costs a few soles. Agree the price before you set off, as taxis have no meters.

By colectivo

Shared minibuses called colectivos leave from Calle Pavitos for the towns of the Sacred Valley, such as Urubamba and Pisac, as soon as they fill; the ride to Urubamba takes about 90 minutes.

The Qorikancha, the Inca temple of the sun, has fine stone walls inside the Dominican monastery that was built over it.

Sacsayhuamán, the fortress on the hill above the city, is built of huge stones fitted without mortar; walk up in 30 minutes from the Plaza de Armas or take a taxi.

Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel, lies about 75 km north-west. Trains run from Poroy station, 20 minutes from the city, and from Ollantaytambo in the Sacred Valley to Aguas Calientes; buses then climb the last 8 km to the ruins. Entry tickets are limited each day and must be bought in advance.

Yellowstone National Park

Yellowstone National Park

Yellowstone National Park, the first national park in the world, covers nearly 9,000 square kilometres of the Rocky Mountains in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho, with more geysers and hot springs than anywhere else on Earth.

Understand

The park sits on top of a supervolcano whose last great eruption, 640,000 years ago, left a caldera 70 km across. The heat below drives Old Faithful and some ten thousand other thermal features.

Most roads and lodges open from late April or May to early November. In winter only the road between the north and north-east entrances is kept open to cars; the interior is reached by snowcoach or snowmobile.

The park's visitor centers have exhibits, maps and rangers who answer questions. The largest is the Old Faithful Visitor Education Center, which posts the predicted time of the next eruption. Albright Visitor Center at Mammoth Hot Springs is open all year.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Fees and permits

A private vehicle pass costs $35 and is good for seven days. Backcountry camping and fishing need separate permits from a ranger station.

Get in

By plane

The closest airports are Yellowstone Airport in West Yellowstone, open in summer only, and Cody, Bozeman and Jackson Hole, all one to two hours from an entrance.

By car

There are five entrances. The North Entrance at Gardiner and the West Entrance at West Yellowstone are the busiest; the North Entrance is the only one open to cars all year.

Get around

There is no public transport inside the park. A figure-eight road, the Grand Loop, links the main sights; the whole loop is about 230 km and takes two days to drive with stops.

By car

The speed limit is 45 mph or lower, and traffic stops whenever animals are near the road. Fill up the tank where you can; there are only a handful of fuel stations.

On foot

Stay on boardwalks in thermal areas; the crust beside the hot springs is thin and the water below can scald to death.

Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes, sending water up to 55 m into the air.

Grand Prismatic Spring, the largest hot spring in the park, is best seen from the overlook trail above it.

The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone has two waterfalls, the Lower Falls being 94 m high.

Lamar Valley, in the north-east, is the best place to see bison and wolves at dawn and dusk.
