Zanzibar

Zanzibar

Zanzibar is an archipelago off the coast of Tanzania, and the name is also used for its main island, Unguja, with the old trading city of Stone Town on its west coast.

Understand

For centuries Zanzibar was the centre of a trade in spices, ivory and enslaved people that ran along the coast of East Africa, and from 1840 it was the seat of the Sultan of Oman. Its old town of coral-stone houses, carved wooden doors and narrow lanes is a World Heritage Site.

Zanzibar is part of Tanzania but has its own government, and visitors arriving from the mainland show their passports again at the port and airport.

Most people are Muslim. Away from the beach resorts, cover your shoulders and knees, and in the holy month of Ramadan do not eat or drink in the street by day.

The Zanzibar Commission for Tourism has an information office on Creek Road in Stone Town.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ) is 8 km south-east of Stone Town, with flights from Dar es Salaam, Arusha, Nairobi and the Gulf. A taxi to Stone Town takes 20 minutes.

By boat

Fast ferries from Dar es Salaam take about two hours and dock at the port in Stone Town; buy tickets only at the ferry company offices inside the terminal gate, not from touts outside.

Visitors must pay a port fee and show a passport on arrival.

Get around

By dala-dala

Dala-dalas, open trucks with benches, run from the Darajani market in Stone Town to every part of the island; the ride to the east coast takes about two hours.

By taxi

Taxis and private minibuses can be hired for the day; a transfer from Stone Town to Nungwi, at the northern tip, takes about an hour and a quarter.

By scooter

Scooters can be hired, but you need an international driving permit and a local permit from the police, and checkpoints are frequent.

See

The House of Wonders, the old sultan's palace on the seafront, was the first building in East Africa with electricity and a lift.

The Old Slave Market site, now a memorial and museum beside the Anglican cathedral, tells the history of the slave trade.

Jozani Forest, in the south of the island, is the only home of the red colobus monkey; guided walks start at the reserve office.

  • Lookout Park, the cathedral square. A hilltop park with a viewpoint over the rooftops and the bay; the path up takes about twenty minutes and there is a cafe at the top.
  • Customs House Gallery, Station Road. The old customs house, now an art gallery with changing exhibitions of modern painting and photography; closed on Mondays.
  • Botanical Garden, Temple Lane. A botanical garden laid out in the colonial period, with shady avenues of palms and a pond of giant water lilies.
  • Old Monastery, the bus stand road. A working monastery whose courtyard and frescoed chapel are open to visitors in the morning; dress modestly and keep your voice down.
  • City Walls, the old harbour road. The city walls, of which a long stretch survives along the river; you can walk along the top for about a kilometre.

Do

Take a spice tour of the farms in the centre of the island, where guides show cloves, nutmeg, vanilla and cinnamon growing.

Swim and snorkel off the beaches of Nungwi and Kendwa, where the tide does not go far out.

  • Public baths, the cathedral square. Spend an afternoon at the public baths, which have hot pools, a steam room and a cafe.
  • Free walking tour, Station Road. Join a free walking tour that leaves from the main square at 10AM daily; the guides work for tips.
  • Market cooking class, Temple Lane. Take a cooking class in a family kitchen, with a trip to the market to buy the ingredients first.
  • Riverside cycling, the bus stand road. Hire a bicycle and ride the flat riverside path out to the villages and back in a morning.

Buy

Tanzanian shillings are used, but hotels, dive shops and tour companies quote in US dollars; bring notes printed after 2009, as older ones are refused.

Eat

The night food market in the Forodhani Gardens, on the seafront of Stone Town, sells grilled seafood, sugarcane juice and Zanzibar pizza, a stuffed and fried pancake.

  • Green Leaf, the cathedral square, mains US$7. Vegetarian dishes, fresh juices and a quiet back room with fans; the owners speak some English.
  • Grill on the Square, Station Road, mains US$9. A grill house on the corner with plastic tables on the pavement; the mixed platter feeds two hungry people.
  • Morning Bakery, Temple Lane, mains US$11. Bakery and coffee shop with pastries, sandwiches and free wifi, handy for breakfast before an early bus.
  • The Townhouse, the bus stand road, mains US$13. An upmarket restaurant in a restored townhouse with a long wine list; book a table at weekends.
  • Harbour Fish Grill, the old harbour road, mains US$15. Seafood fresh from the harbour, sold by weight; agree the price before it goes on the grill.

Drink

Bars and cafes stay open late in the centre, and the local beer is cheap.

  • The Lantern Pub, the cathedral square. A small pub with live music on Friday and Saturday nights and cheap local beer on tap.
  • Courtyard Tea House, Station Road. A tea house in an old courtyard, serving dozens of teas and small sweets in the afternoon.
  • River Brewing, Temple Lane. A craft brewery near the river with long tables and a food truck outside in the evenings.

Sleep

Stone Town has guesthouses in old merchant houses, while the resorts are on the north and east coasts.

  • The Waterfront, the cathedral square, from US$85. A grand hotel of the 1920s on the waterfront, with high ceilings, a famous bar and prices to match.
  • Courtyard Guesthouse, Station Road, from US$25. Rooms with fans or air conditioning around a small courtyard; breakfast is included and the owner arranges taxis.
  • Grand Plaza Hotel, Temple Lane, from US$40. A large modern hotel with a pool, a gym and a shuttle to the airport every hour.
  • Teacher's House, the bus stand road, from US$55. A quiet guesthouse in a side street run by a retired teacher; book ahead in the high season.

Stay safe

Do not walk alone on empty beaches or in the lanes of Stone Town late at night, where muggings have happened.

Beach boys offering tours and boat trips can be persistent; book through your hotel.

Connect

Prepaid SIM cards are sold at the airport and at phone shops in the centre; bring your passport, which is needed to register the card.

Most hotels, cafes and many restaurants have free wifi.

Go next

Pemba — the quieter northern island, by small plane or ferry.

Dar es Salaam — two hours by fast ferry.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2024-01/A/Cartage:
Cartagena (Colombia)

Cartagena (Colombia)

Cartagena de Indias is a port on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, famous for its walled old city of balconied colonial houses, churches and plazas.

Understand

The Spanish founded the city in 1533, and its harbour became the main port for the silver and gold shipped from South America to Spain. The walls and forts were built to keep out pirates and the fleets of rival empires.

The old city is divided into the walled centre, San Diego and Getsemaní; Bocagrande, a peninsula of high-rise hotels and beaches, lies to the south.

A tourist card is not needed for most nationalities; visitors are stamped in on arrival for up to 90 days and must fill in the online migration form, Check-MIG, within 72 hours before the flight.

Hotels add a tourist tax of a few thousand pesos per night to the bill, which goes to the city.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

By plane

Rafael Núñez International Airport (CTG) is 3 km north-east of the old city. Taxis from the official rank cost a fixed fare posted on a board; the ride takes 15 minutes.

By bus

Long-distance buses arrive at the bus station on the edge of the city, 45 minutes from the centre by taxi or by the TransCaribe bus. Buses to Santa Marta take about five hours.

Get around

On foot

The walled city is small and best explored on foot, early in the morning or late in the afternoon when it is cooler.

By taxi

Taxis have no meters; ask the price before you get in. A short ride within the centre costs about the same everywhere, and fares rise at night.

By bus

TransCaribe buses run on dedicated lanes from the bus station to the old city; buy a card at a station before you board.

See

The Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the largest Spanish fort in the Americas, guards the land approach; go early to avoid the heat.

The Palace of the Inquisition, on Plaza Bolívar, is now a museum of the city's history.

  • Customs House Gallery, the main square. The old customs house, now an art gallery with changing exhibitions of modern painting and photography; closed on Mondays.
  • Botanical Garden, the north gate. A botanical garden laid out in the colonial period, with shady avenues of palms and a pond of giant water lilies.
  • Old Monastery, the cathedral square. A working monastery whose courtyard and frescoed chapel are open to visitors in the morning; dress modestly and keep your voice down.
  • City Walls, Station Road. The city walls, of which a long stretch survives along the river; you can walk along the top for about a kilometre.
  • Town Museum, Temple Lane. A small museum of local history in a merchant's house, with old maps, costumes and photographs of the town a century ago; labels are in English and the local language.

Do

Take a boat to the Rosario Islands for snorkelling over coral reefs; boats leave from the Muelle de la Bodeguita pier at 8AM.

Walk the top of the city walls at sunset.

  • City stadium, the main square. Watch a football match at the city stadium, where tickets are cheap and the crowd is loud.
  • Public baths, the north gate. Spend an afternoon at the public baths, which have hot pools, a steam room and a cafe.
  • Free walking tour, the cathedral square. Join a free walking tour that leaves from the main square at 10AM daily; the guides work for tips.
  • Market cooking class, Station Road. Take a cooking class in a family kitchen, with a trip to the market to buy the ingredients first.

Buy

Pay in pesos; small shops and street vendors do not take cards or dollars. Use ATMs inside banks or shopping centres, as card skimmers have been found on street machines.

Eat

Arepas de huevo, fried corn cakes with an egg inside, are the classic street snack. Fresh fish with coconut rice and fried plantain is served all along the coast.

  • Grill on the Square, the main square, mains US$9. A grill house on the corner with plastic tables on the pavement; the mixed platter feeds two hungry people.
  • Morning Bakery, the north gate, mains US$11. Bakery and coffee shop with pastries, sandwiches and free wifi, handy for breakfast before an early bus.
  • The Townhouse, the cathedral square, mains US$13. An upmarket restaurant in a restored townhouse with a long wine list; book a table at weekends.
  • Harbour Fish Grill, Station Road, mains US$15. Seafood fresh from the harbour, sold by weight; agree the price before it goes on the grill.
  • Mama's Kitchen, Temple Lane, mains US$3. A family-run place with a short menu of local dishes; the lunch set is good value and the queue moves quickly.

Drink

Bars and cafes stay open late in the centre, and the local beer is cheap.

  • River Brewing, the main square. A craft brewery near the river with long tables and a food truck outside in the evenings.
  • Sky Terrace, the north gate. A rooftop bar with views over the old town; cocktails are pricey but the sunset is free.
  • The Lantern Pub, the cathedral square. A small pub with live music on Friday and Saturday nights and cheap local beer on tap.

Sleep

Getsemaní has the most hostels and cheap guesthouses; the boutique hotels are in the walled city.

  • Station Business Hotel, the main square, from US$70. Business hotel near the main station with small but clean rooms and a buffet breakfast.
  • The Waterfront, the north gate, from US$85. A grand hotel of the 1920s on the waterfront, with high ceilings, a famous bar and prices to match.
  • Courtyard Guesthouse, the cathedral square, from US$25. Rooms with fans or air conditioning around a small courtyard; breakfast is included and the owner arranges taxis.
  • Grand Plaza Hotel, Station Road, from US$40. A large modern hotel with a pool, a gym and a shuttle to the airport every hour.

Stay safe

The old city and Bocagrande are patrolled by the tourist police, who wear green vests and have a booth on Plaza de los Coches; they speak some English.

Pickpockets work in crowds, and some street vendors and touts pressure visitors hard. Do not accept drinks from strangers in bars, as drugging and robbery have been reported.

Emergency number: 123 for police, ambulance and fire.

Stay healthy

The heat and humidity are intense; drink plenty of water and use sunscreen. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes, so use repellent.

Connect

Prepaid SIM cards are sold at the airport and at phone shops in the centre; bring your passport, which is needed to register the card.

Most hotels, cafes and many restaurants have free wifi.

Go next

Santa Marta — a beach town near the Sierra Nevada, five hours by bus.

Rosario Islands — coral islands an hour by boat.

Antigua Guatemala

Antigua Guatemala

Antigua Guatemala is a colonial town in the central highlands of Guatemala, ringed by three volcanoes and known for its cobbled streets, ruined churches and Spanish-language schools.

Understand

Antigua was the Spanish capital of Central America until earthquakes in 1773 destroyed much of it and the capital moved to Guatemala City. Many of the churches were never rebuilt and stand as ruins.

Volcán de Agua, south of town, is dormant; Volcán de Fuego, to the west, erupts almost every day, and its glow can be seen at night from the town.

The town is at 1,500 m, with warm days and cool nights all year. The rainy season runs from May to October.

INGUAT, the tourist board, has an office on the Parque Central with maps and bus times.

The population has grown fast since the 1980s as people moved in from the countryside, and new suburbs of apartment blocks now ring the old centre on every side.

Most signs in the centre are in the local language and in English, but few people outside the hotels and the main sights speak much English; a phrasebook or a translation app helps.

The main festival falls in the spring, when the streets fill with processions and music for a week and hotel prices double; book well ahead if you plan to be there then.

Get in

Shuttle minibuses run from La Aurora airport in Guatemala City, about an hour away, and from Lake Atitlán, about three hours.

Chicken buses, old American school buses painted in bright colours, run from Guatemala City every few minutes; they are cheap but crowded.

Get around

The centre is a grid of streets that is easy to walk; the cobbles are uneven.

Tuk-tuks wait around the Parque Central for short rides.

See

The ruins of La Recolección and the cathedral show the scale of the colonial town.

The yellow arch of Santa Catalina, over Fifth Avenue North, is the town's best-known sight.

  • Botanical Garden, the river embankment. A botanical garden laid out in the colonial period, with shady avenues of palms and a pond of giant water lilies.
  • Old Monastery, Hill Road. A working monastery whose courtyard and frescoed chapel are open to visitors in the morning; dress modestly and keep your voice down.
  • City Walls, Market Street. The city walls, of which a long stretch survives along the river; you can walk along the top for about a kilometre.
  • Town Museum, the main square. A small museum of local history in a merchant's house, with old maps, costumes and photographs of the town a century ago; labels are in English and the local language.
  • Market Hall, the north gate. A covered market hall of iron and glass from the 1890s, busiest early in the morning when the fishmongers and fruit sellers set up.

Do

Climb Volcán de Acatenango, beside Fuego, on an overnight hike with a guide to watch Fuego erupt; the climb gains 1,500 m and is very cold at the top.

Take a hike up Volcán Pacaya, a shorter climb to an active cone where you can see old lava flows.

Study Spanish at one of dozens of schools, many with homestays.

  • Public baths, the river embankment. Spend an afternoon at the public baths, which have hot pools, a steam room and a cafe.
  • Free walking tour, Hill Road. Join a free walking tour that leaves from the main square at 10AM daily; the guides work for tips.
  • Market cooking class, Market Street. Take a cooking class in a family kitchen, with a trip to the market to buy the ingredients first.
  • Riverside cycling, the main square. Hire a bicycle and ride the flat riverside path out to the villages and back in a morning.

Buy

The handicraft market by the bus terminal sells textiles woven in the highland villages; bargain politely.

Eat

Pepián, a thick stew of meat and vegetables, is the national dish. Black beans, tortillas and eggs make the usual breakfast.

  • Morning Bakery, the river embankment, mains US$11. Bakery and coffee shop with pastries, sandwiches and free wifi, handy for breakfast before an early bus.
  • The Townhouse, Hill Road, mains US$13. An upmarket restaurant in a restored townhouse with a long wine list; book a table at weekends.
  • Harbour Fish Grill, Market Street, mains US$15. Seafood fresh from the harbour, sold by weight; agree the price before it goes on the grill.
  • Mama's Kitchen, the main square, mains US$3. A family-run place with a short menu of local dishes; the lunch set is good value and the queue moves quickly.
  • Corner Noodle House, the north gate, mains US$5. Popular with office workers at lunchtime for its noodle soups and grilled meats; go early or late to get a table.

Drink

Bars and cafes stay open late in the centre, and the local beer is cheap.

  • Sky Terrace, the river embankment. A rooftop bar with views over the old town; cocktails are pricey but the sunset is free.
  • The Lantern Pub, Hill Road. A small pub with live music on Friday and Saturday nights and cheap local beer on tap.
  • Courtyard Tea House, Market Street. A tea house in an old courtyard, serving dozens of teas and small sweets in the afternoon.

Sleep

  • Volcano View Backpackers, 4a Calle Poniente, dorm Q80. Dorms of eight beds, a rooftop terrace facing Agua and a shared kitchen.
  • Casa del Arco, 5a Avenida Norte, Q350. A small hotel in a colonial house near the arch.
  • The Waterfront, the river embankment, from US$85. A grand hotel of the 1920s on the waterfront, with high ceilings, a famous bar and prices to match.
  • Courtyard Guesthouse, Hill Road, from US$25. Rooms with fans or air conditioning around a small courtyard; breakfast is included and the owner arranges taxis.
  • Grand Plaza Hotel, Market Street, from US$40. A large modern hotel with a pool, a gym and a shuttle to the airport every hour.
  • Teacher's House, the main square, from US$55. A quiet guesthouse in a side street run by a retired teacher; book ahead in the high season.

Stay safe

Keep your backpack in front of you on chicken buses and in the market, where thieves slit bags.

Hike the volcanoes only with a registered guide; armed robbers have attacked hikers on lonely trails, and the weather on Acatenango can turn dangerous.

Do not walk alone after dark outside the centre.

Connect

Prepaid SIM cards are sold at the airport and at phone shops in the centre; bring your passport, which is needed to register the card.

Most hotels, cafes and many restaurants have free wifi.

Go next

Lake Atitlán — a volcanic lake ringed with villages, three hours by shuttle.

Guatemala City — an hour by bus or shuttle.

ThinkPad T480 Fan Replacement

Written By: Sam Ortega
  • Comments7

Difficulty

Moderate

Steps

12

Time Required

45 minutes - 1 hour

Introduction

Use this guide to replace a noisy or failed cooling fan in a ThinkPad T480.

The fan and heat sink come out as one assembly. You will need to clean off the old thermal paste and apply new paste before you put the heat sink back.

Tools

  • Phillips #0 Screwdriver

  • Spudger

  • iFixit Opening Picks (Set of 6)

  • Isopropyl Alcohol

  • Arctic Silver ArctiClean

Parts

  • ThinkPad T480 Fan Assembly

  • Thermal Paste

  1. Step 1

    • Before you begin, shut down the laptop and unplug the charger.

    • Turn the laptop over and close the lid so it lies flat on a soft surface.

    • Disable the built-in battery in the BIOS under Config > Power before you open the case.

    Disabling the battery in the BIOS is really important, I fried a board once by skipping it.

    Ken R - Mar 3, 2023

    Where is that menu on the newer BIOS?

    Lia - Mar 3, 2023

  2. Step 2

    • Loosen the eight captive Phillips screws on the bottom cover.

    • The screws stay in the cover; do not try to remove them completely.

  3. Step 3

    • Insert an opening pick between the bottom cover and the case near the hinge.

    • Slide the pick along the edge to release the clips.

    • Lift the bottom cover off the laptop.

    The clips at the front are very tight, I used two picks.

    dan - Mar 3, 2023

  4. Step 4

    • Disconnect the internal battery connector by pulling it straight up from the motherboard.

    • Never pry against the battery itself; a damaged battery can catch fire.

  5. Step 5

    • Remove the two 4.5 mm Phillips screws securing the internal battery.

    • Lift the battery out of the laptop.

  6. Step 6

    • Use the tip of a spudger to pry the fan cable connector straight up off its socket on the motherboard.

    Mine came with tape over the connector, peel it first.

    Rafa - Mar 3, 2023

  7. Step 7

    • Loosen the four captive screws on the heat sink in the order printed next to each screw: 4, 3, 2, 1.

    • Remove the two 2.5 mm Phillips screws securing the fan to the frame.

  8. Step 8

    • Lift the fan and heat sink assembly out of the laptop.

    • The thermal paste may hold the heat sink to the processor. Twist it gently to break the seal; do not pull hard.

  9. Step 9

    • Wipe the old thermal paste from the processor and the heat sink with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth.

    • Let the surfaces dry completely.

    Don't use paper towels, they leave fibres everywhere.

    anon - Mar 3, 2023

  10. Step 10

    • Apply a pea-sized drop of new thermal paste to the centre of the processor.

    • Do not spread the paste; the heat sink will spread it when you tighten the screws.

  11. Step 11

    • Lower the new fan assembly into place and tighten the heat sink screws in the order 1, 2, 3, 4.

    • Reconnect the fan cable.

  12. Step 12

    • To reassemble your device, follow these instructions in reverse order.

    Worked great, temps dropped 15 degrees!

    Mo - Mar 3, 2023

    Took me two hours but the fan is silent now.

    Ty - Mar 3, 2023

Conclusion

To reassemble your device, follow these instructions in reverse order.

Turn the battery back on by plugging in the charger once the cover is closed.

Google Pixel 5a Battery Replacement

Written By: Sam Ortega
  • Comments7

Difficulty

Difficult

Steps

11

Time Required

1 - 2 hours

Introduction

This guide shows how to replace the battery in a Google Pixel 5a.

If your battery is swollen, take appropriate precautions. Do not heat a swollen battery.

For your safety, discharge the battery below 25% before you take the phone apart. This lowers the risk of a dangerous thermal event if the battery is damaged during the repair.

Tools

  • iOpener

  • Suction Handle

  • iFixit Opening Picks

  • Spudger

  • Tweezers

  • Phillips #000 Screwdriver

Parts

  • Pixel 5a Battery

  • Pixel 5a Screen Adhesive

  1. Step 1

    • Power off the phone completely.

    • Heat an iOpener and apply it to the left edge of the screen for two minutes.

    • Do not overheat the phone. The display and the battery are sensitive to heat; the edge should be too hot to touch comfortably, about 80 °C, and no hotter.

    A hair dryer works fine too if you don't have an iOpener.

    Joe - Mar 3, 2023

  2. Step 2

    • Press a suction handle onto the heated edge of the screen.

    • Pull up on the handle with firm, steady force to make a small gap.

    • Insert an opening pick into the gap.

  3. Step 3

    • Insert the pick no more than 3 mm, or you may damage the display cable on the right edge.

    • Slide the pick around the bottom corner to slice the adhesive.

    • Leave the pick in place to keep the adhesive from sealing again.

    I went too deep and cut the display cable, read the warning!

    Nina - Mar 3, 2023

  4. Step 4

    • Repeat the heating and slicing on the top and right edges.

    • Swing the screen open from the left like a book.

  5. Step 5

    • Remove the four 3.2 mm Phillips screws securing the display cable cover.

    • Lift the cover off with tweezers.

  6. Step 6

    • Use a spudger to disconnect the display cable by prying it straight up.

    • Remove the screen.

  7. Step 7

    • Remove the six screws securing the midframe.

    • Lift the midframe from the bottom edge and remove it.

    One of the six screws is hidden under a sticker near the camera.

    Ali - Mar 3, 2023

  8. Step 8

    • Disconnect the battery connector with the flat end of a spudger.

    Before this step cover the battery terminal with tape, mine shorted against the frame and sparked.

    Theo - Mar 3, 2023

    Also keep the old battery in a metal box until you recycle it, a punctured battery can reignite hours later.

    Jo - Mar 3, 2023

  9. Step 9

    • Pull the two black adhesive tabs at the bottom of the battery slowly and evenly at a low angle.

    • If a tab breaks, apply a few drops of isopropyl alcohol under the battery and wait two minutes for the adhesive to soften.

    • Do not bend or puncture the battery with your tools.

  10. Step 10

    • Lift out the old battery.

    • Press the new battery firmly into place for 30 seconds.

  11. Step 11

    • Clean the old screen adhesive from the frame and apply new adhesive.

    • Reconnect the display and press the screen down along all edges.

    • Clamp the screen or stack books on it for an hour while the new adhesive sets.

Conclusion

Compare your new replacement part to the original part before you install it.

Take your old battery to an e-waste recycler; do not put it in the household rubbish.

pages.ifixit_en_all_2024-01/Guide/Washing_Mach:
Front-Loading Washing Machine Drain Pump Replacement

Written By: Sam Ortega
  • Comments7

Difficulty

Moderate

Steps

9

Time Required

1 - 2 hours

Introduction

If your washer stops mid-cycle with water still in the drum, or hums without draining, the drain pump may be blocked or failed.

This guide covers a common front-loading design. Unplug the machine and turn off the water taps before you start, and have towels and a shallow tray ready: up to 10 litres of water can come out of the pump.

Tools

  • Flathead Screwdriver

  • Torx T20 Screwdriver

  • Pliers

  • Shallow tray

Parts

  • Drain Pump

  1. Step 1

    • Unplug the washing machine from the wall socket. Water and mains electricity are a deadly combination.

    • Turn off both water taps behind the machine.

  2. Step 2

    • Open the small service flap at the bottom right of the front panel.

    • Place a shallow tray under the emergency drain hose.

    My flap was on the left side, depends on the model.

    Ola - Mar 3, 2023

  3. Step 3

    • Pull out the emergency drain hose, remove its cap and let the water drain into the tray.

    • Empty the tray as often as needed; the drain can take ten minutes.

  4. Step 4

    • Unscrew the pump filter anticlockwise and pull it out.

    • Remove any coins, hair clips or lint caught in the filter or the pump opening.

    • Check that the impeller inside the opening turns freely by hand. If it is jammed or broken, the pump must be replaced.

    Found a sock in mine. No need to replace anything after that.

    Bo - Mar 3, 2023

  5. Step 5

    • Remove the three T20 Torx screws along the bottom edge of the front kick plate and take the plate off.

  6. Step 6

    • Lay the machine on its left side on an old blanket, with a helper.

    • The machine weighs about 70 kg; do not lift it alone.

  7. Step 7

    • Disconnect the wiring plug from the pump by pressing the release tab.

    • Loosen the hose clamps with pliers and pull the two hoses off the pump.

Introduction

Replace the front brake pads when they are worn to 3 mm or when the wear indicator squeals.

  • Torque Wrench

Parts

  • Front Brake Pads

  • Brake Grease

  1. Step 1

    • Park on level ground, set the parking brake and loosen the lug nuts a half turn while the wheel is still on the ground.

  2. Step 2

    • Lift the front of the car with a floor jack at the jacking point and set it on jack stands.

    • Never work under a car held up only by a jack.

  3. Step 3

    • Remove the lug nuts and the wheel.

  4. Step 4

    • Remove the two 14 mm caliper slide bolts.

    • Swing the caliper up and away from the rotor and hang it with a wire or zip tie.

    • Do not let the caliper hang by its brake hose.

  5. Step 5

    • Slide the old pads out of the caliper bracket.

    • Remove the anti-rattle clips and clean the bracket with a wire brush.

  6. Step 6

    • Use a C-clamp and an old pad to push the caliper piston slowly back into its bore.

    • Open the brake fluid reservoir cap first and watch the level; fluid can overflow and it damages paint.

  7. Step 7

    • Fit new anti-rattle clips, put a thin film of brake grease on the pad ears and slide in the new pads.

  8. Step 8

    • Swing the caliper down over the pads and tighten the slide bolts to 34 N·m (25 ft·lb).

  9. Step 9

    • Refit the wheel, lower the car and tighten the lug nuts to 103 N·m (76 ft·lb) in a star pattern.

    • Before you drive, sit in the car and step on the brake pedal slowly several times until it feels firm.

    • Check the brake fluid level and top it up to the MAX line.

    • Bed in the new pads: make about ten moderate stops from 50 km/h to 10 km/h without stopping completely, then drive for a few minutes without braking to let them cool.

Peru, officially the Republic of Peru, is a country in western South America.[220] It is bordered by Ecuador and Colombia to the north, Brazil to the east, Bolivia to the south-east, Chile to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. It is a megadiverse country, with habitats ranging from the arid plains of the Pacific coast to the peaks of the Andes and the tropical rainforest of the Amazon basin.

Peruvian territory was home to some of the oldest civilisations of the Americas, among them Caral, and later to the Inca Empire, the largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas.[221] The Spanish conquered the Incas in the sixteenth century and ruled from Lima until independence in 1821. Today Peru is a democratic republic of about 34 million people, and its economy rests on mining, fishing, farming and tourism.

Etymology

[edit]

The name Peru probably comes from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama in the early sixteenth century, whose lands the Spanish took to be the edge of a rich southern kingdom.[222]

History

[edit]

Early cultures

[edit]

The city of Caral, on the coast north of Lima, was built around 2600 BC and is one of the oldest cities in the Americas.[223] Later cultures included the Chavín, the Nazca, famous for the giant lines drawn on the desert, the Moche and the Chimú.

Inca Empire

[edit]

The Incas built their empire from Cusco in the fifteenth century, and at its height it stretched 4,000 km along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile.[224] It was run without writing, using knotted cords called quipu to keep records, and linked by a road network of about 40,000 km.

Spanish conquest

[edit]

Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532 and had him executed the next year.[225] Epidemics of smallpox and other diseases brought from Europe killed a large part of the population.

Independence

[edit]

José de San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence in Lima on 28 July 1821, and the last Spanish forces were defeated at the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824.[226]

Twentieth century

[edit]

The country alternated between elected governments and military rule.[227] From 1980 to 2000 the Shining Path insurgency and the army's response cost about 70,000 lives, most of them rural Quechua speakers.

Geography

[edit]

Peru is divided into three main regions: the narrow coastal desert, the Andean highlands, and the Amazon rainforest, which covers about 60 percent of the country.[228]

Coast

[edit]

The coast is one of the driest deserts on Earth, crossed by about fifty rivers that flow down from the Andes and water oases of farmland.[229] Lima and most other large cities are on the coast.

Andes

[edit]

The Andes run the length of the country, and Huascarán, at 6,768 m, is the highest peak in Peru.[230] Lake Titicaca, on the border with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America by volume and lies at 3,812 m.

Amazon

[edit]

East of the Andes the land falls to the Amazon basin, where the Marañón and Ucayali rivers join to form the Amazon.[231] Iquitos, the largest city in the world that cannot be reached by road, lies on the river.

Climate

[edit]

The cold Humboldt Current off the coast cools the air above the sea, so that it holds little moisture and almost no rain falls on the coast, which is covered instead by a grey sea fog from June to October.[232] Every few years El Niño brings warm water and heavy rain and floods to the north coast.

Government and politics

[edit]

Government

[edit]

Peru is a presidential republic. The president is elected for five years and cannot serve two terms in a row; Congress has a single chamber of 130 members.[233]

Administrative divisions

[edit]

The country is divided into 24 departments and the constitutional province of Callao.[234]

Economy

[edit]

Peru's economy grew quickly from the early 2000s, and poverty fell from more than half of the population to about a quarter.[235]

Mining

[edit]

Mining provides about 60 percent of exports.[236] Peru is the world's second-largest producer of copper and silver, and a large producer of gold and zinc.

Fishing

[edit]

The cold, nutrient-rich water of the Humboldt Current supports one of the richest fisheries in the world, mainly of anchovies, which are ground into fishmeal for animal feed.[237]

Agriculture

[edit]

Peru is a major exporter of asparagus, avocados, blueberries and coffee.[238] The potato was first domesticated in the Andes of southern Peru, and farmers there grow thousands of varieties.

Tourism

[edit]

Tourism, centred on Machu Picchu, Cusco and the Amazon, is the third-largest industry.[239]

Demographics

[edit]

Population

[edit]

About a third of Peruvians live in the Lima metropolitan area.[240] Most people are mestizo, of mixed Amerindian and European ancestry; Quechua and Aymara peoples are the largest Amerindian groups.

Languages

[edit]

Spanish is spoken by about 83 percent of the population as a first language and Quechua by about 13 percent.[241] Aymara and many Amazonian languages are official in the areas where they are spoken.

Religion

[edit]

Most Peruvians are Roman Catholic, and evangelical Protestant churches have grown since the 1980s.[242]

Culture

[edit]

Cuisine

[edit]

Ceviche, raw fish cured in lime juice with chili and onion, is the national dish.[243] Peruvian cooking mixes Amerindian, Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese influences; chifa, Chinese-Peruvian food, is found in every town.

Music

[edit]

Andean music is played on panpipes, the quena flute and the charango, a small lute.[244] The cajón, a box drum, came from the music of Afro-Peruvians on the coast.

Sport

[edit]

Football is the most popular sport; Peru won the Copa América in 1939 and 1975.[245]

The recovery position keeps the airway of an unconscious person who is breathing open, and lets fluid drain from the mouth instead of being breathed in. Use it only for a person who is breathing normally; if they are not breathing, call for emergency help and start CPR.

Before you start

Check that the area is safe for you and the casualty. Call for help or send someone to call the emergency number, and ask for an automated external defibrillator if one is near.

If you suspect an injury to the neck or spine, such as after a fall from a height or a road crash, move the person only if you must to keep the airway open.

Procedure

  1. Step 1

    Kneel beside the person, who is lying on their back. Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to their body, palm up.

  2. Step 2

    Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against the cheek nearest you.

  3. Step 3

    With your other hand, lift the far knee so that the foot is flat on the ground.

    Pull on the bent knee to roll the person toward you onto their side.

  4. Step 4

    Tilt the head back gently and lift the chin to keep the airway open. Adjust the hand under the cheek if needed.

    Check breathing every minute until help arrives; if breathing stops, roll them onto their back and start CPR.

If you have to leave the person to get help, put them in the recovery position first.

Children and babies

A child over one year is placed in the same position as an adult. A baby under one year should be held in your arms with the head tilted down, so the tongue cannot block the throat and vomit can drain.

Pregnancy

A heavily pregnant woman should be placed on her left side, so that the womb does not press on the large vein that returns blood to the heart.

A small emergency kit carried on every trip can turn a dangerous night into an uncomfortable one. Each item below earns its place by weight.

Items

  • Whistle

    Three short blasts, repeated, is the call for help; a whistle carries farther than a voice and costs no strength.

  • Space blanket

    A thin foil sheet that reflects body heat; wrap it around the body under a coat, not over wet clothes.

  • Water purification tablets

    Chlorine dioxide tablets treat one litre each; follow the waiting time on the pack, usually 30 minutes, longer in cold or cloudy water.

  • Fire starter

    A ferrocerium rod throws hot sparks even when wet; carry dry tinder in a sealed bag.

  • Headlamp

    A headlamp leaves both hands free; carry spare batteries and keep them warm in cold weather.

Packing

Pack the kit in a waterproof bag and check it before each season; replace tablets and batteries by their dates.

Euclidean algorithm

In mathematics, the Euclidean algorithm is an efficient method for computing the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers, the largest number that divides both without a remainder.[246] It is named after the Greek mathematician Euclid, who described it in his Elements around 300 BC. It is one of the oldest algorithms in common use.

Procedure

[edit]

The algorithm repeats one step until a remainder of zero is reached:

  1. Step 1: Divide the larger number a by the smaller number b and find the remainder r.
  2. Step 2: If r is zero, b is the greatest common divisor, and the algorithm stops.
  3. Step 3: Otherwise, replace a with b and b with r, and go back to step 1.

Example

[edit]

To find the GCD of 1071 and 462: 1071 divided by 462 leaves 147; 462 divided by 147 leaves 21; 147 divided by 21 leaves 0, so the GCD is 21.[247]

Efficiency

[edit]

The number of steps is never more than five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number, a result proved by Gabriel Lamé in 1844.[248]

Applications

[edit]

The algorithm is used to reduce fractions to their simplest form, in the RSA method of public-key cryptography, and to solve Diophantine equations.[249]

English

Etymology

From Middle English brike, from Middle Dutch bricke, a piece or fragment, related to the verb to break.

Pronunciation

  • IPA: /bɹɪk/
  • Rhymes: -ɪk

Noun

brick (countable and uncountable, plural bricks)

  1. A hardened rectangular block of mud, clay or similar material, used for building.
    • The house was built of red brick.
  2. Such blocks as a material.
    a wall of brick
  3. (informal, dated) A helpful and reliable person.
    • Thanks for driving me home, you are a real brick.
  4. (slang) An electronic device that no longer works at all, especially after a failed software update.

Synonyms

  • (device that no longer works): paperweight

Verb

brick (third-person singular simple present bricks, present participle bricking)

  1. To build with bricks.
  2. (slang) To make an electronic device stop working entirely, as by a failed update of its firmware.
    • The update bricked my router, so I had to send it back.

  • A dictionary of the English language, second edition, 1989.
